title: The Greenhouse Auction
scenes: Scene 1. Hendrik Maas, who had spent forty years and most of a fortune on orchids, is found dead in the study of his glass-roofed house on the morning his collection was to be auctioned. A cup of tea stands on the desk, half drunk. The gardener, Pim de Wit, had been treating the greenhouse for aphids all week with a nicotine extract he mixes himself; the smell of it hangs in the corridor. Hendrik's sister Greta, who runs the house, finds the body at eight and telephones the auctioneer before she telephones a doctor.

Scene 2. Benedikt Roos, the auctioneer, arrives at nine with the catalogue. The sale was his idea: Hendrik's debts had reached the point where the collection had to go. Roos stands to earn a commission of twelve percent on a sale expected to bring four hundred thousand. He is shaken, or performs it well, and asks whether the sale can proceed 'as the estate would surely want'.

Scene 3. Pim de Wit is questioned in the potting shed. He says he brought Hendrik his tea at seven as always, left it outside the study door and never went in; 'the study is not my place, I have never set foot in it'. He mentions the aphid treatment without being asked and says the extract is kept locked in the shed. His boots are caked with the red clay of the orchid beds.

Scene 4. Yuna Park, the botanist Hendrik had hired to catalogue the collection, says she worked in the greenhouse until midnight and slept in the guest wing. She disliked the auction: three of the plants are, in her view, the last of their kind in cultivation, and she had tried to persuade Hendrik to give them to a botanical garden instead. She had argued with him the evening before, loudly enough for Greta to hear.

Scene 5. The doctor, when he finally comes, says the death is consistent with poisoning and that the tea should be kept. Greta says the tea was Hendrik's usual, made in the kitchen by her, carried up by Pim. The inspector walks the house. On the pale rug of the study, just inside the door, there are two faint prints of red clay, recently brushed at.

Scene 6. Rafael Ortega, the buyer who had flown in for the sale, had made Hendrik a private offer for the whole collection a month earlier, which Hendrik refused. Ortega says he would gain nothing from Hendrik's death, since the auction raises prices. He admits he was in the house the night before, as a guest, and that he and Hendrik drank brandy together in the study at ten. He saw no one else.

Scene 7. The inspector asks each person what Hendrik drank that morning. Greta: 'his tea, as always'. Roos: 'I was not here'. Park: 'coffee, I suppose, like the rest of us'. Ortega: 'tea, I was told'. Pim de Wit: 'Earl Grey, with the bergamot, he liked it strong'. Nobody in the house has said what kind of tea it was, and the tin in the kitchen is unlabelled.

Scene 8. Greta shows the inspector the household ledger. Pim de Wit's wages are three months in arrears; Hendrik had told him the week before that he would be let go after the sale, with nothing. There is also a note of a loan of eight hundred Hendrik made to Pim two years ago, never repaid, with 'to be deducted' written against it in Hendrik's hand.

Scene 9. The analysis comes back: nicotine, in a concentration no cigarette could give, in the tea and in the dregs of the cup. The shed is opened. The extract bottle is there, locked as Pim said, but the level is a finger lower than the mark Pim himself had scratched on the glass the previous evening, which he had shown the inspector to prove it untouched.

Scene 10. Pim de Wit, confronted with the clay on the study rug, the Earl Grey he could not have known about without entering the study, and the bottle, admits it. He had put the extract in the tea in the corridor, then gone into the study to make sure Hendrik drank it, and brushed at the rug on his way out. He had believed the sale would leave him on the street with the loan still owed. He is arrested before the auction can begin; Roos postpones it.
